<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-argued cases, but A's dialectical trap in Rebuttal 2 (A4.4) — that B's proposed safeguards either collapse into existing reasonable-suspicion law (making "expansion" redundant) or remain a time-and-place dragnet on innocent bystanders — was a sharp, unanswered challenge to B's core proposal. B's answer to the Pressure Questions (concrete triggers plus oversight) was thoughtful and direct, satisfying the format well, but it inadvertently opened this dilemma, which A exploited immediately afterward. B's closing, which needed to resolve this and reassert the asymmetry framing, was clipped for exceeding the word limit, leaving the dilemma unrebutted and B's final case incomplete — a real execution cost per the judging criteria. A also consistently pressed the underexamined assumption in B's mechanism (that seizures causally reduce stabbings rather than merely correlating with them), forcing B to shift the burden back onto A without ever closing the loop on why weaker-threshold search specifically outperforms existing evidence-based powers. B's vivid framing and asymmetry argument (corrigible friction vs. irreversible death) were rhetorically strong and repeated effectively across rounds, and A's rebuttal that lost trust/cooperation is also a potentially irreversible cost was somewhat abstract by comparison — but this exchange remained live rather than decisively won by either side. The tie-breaker is A's unanswered structural critique plus B's incomplete, clipped closing, giving A the cleaner, more complete path to the decision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 point [A4.4] — arguing that B's proposed safeguards either reduce to already-legal individualized suspicion or remain a broad dragnet — was the most decisive unrebutted exchange, compounded by B's closing being clipped before it could respond.</best_rebuttal>
